country.name: Kenya
country.tagline: Equatorial vineyards on the shores of Lake Naivasha, high in the Rift Valley.
country.overview:
Kenya's grape wine is a recent, small-scale story centred on Lake Naivasha in the Rift Valley, about 90 km north-west of Nairobi at about 1,900 m. Altitude moderates the equatorial heat, and the region's horticulture and flower farms supply irrigation know-how. Rift Valley Winery's Leleshwa wines, from vineyards near the lake, are the best known; Kenyans otherwise drink imported wine and locally made fruit wines (the state-founded Kenya Wine Agencies long made papaya-based wine). As on the equator elsewhere, vines can be managed for two crops a year.

Kenya's wine is a niche: high excise and import duties shape the market, and most wine drunk in Kenya is imported from South Africa. The Naivasha vineyards benefit from altitude and Rift Valley sunshine, and are managed for two harvests a year, with the dry-season crop giving the better wine. Kenya Wine Agencies Limited, set up in the 1960s, long made fruit wines, including papaya-based wine, for the domestic market.

history.title: Leleshwa
history.text: Rift Valley Winery began producing Leleshwa wines from vineyards near Lake Naivasha.

history.title: Kenya Wine Agencies
history.text: Kenya Wine Agencies Limited was set up in the 1960s to import and distribute wine and later made fruit wines, including papaya-based wine, for the local market.

country.climate_soils: Equatorial highland climate at about 1,900 m; volcanic soils.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon

sites.name: Lake Naivasha vineyards
sites.text: Vineyards near Lake Naivasha, at about 1,900 m in the Rift Valley, produce Kenya's best-known grape wines (Leleshwa); the lake's flower and vegetable farms share the area's water and volcanic soils.
